### 2.1 Meta-World (meta-world)

`data/benchmarks/robotics-embodiment/meta-world.yaml` · `verification_status: ai-drafted-unverified` · curator confidence medium · added 2026-11-04 · last verified 2026-11-04

*50 simulated Sawyer-arm manipulation tasks in multi-task and meta-RL task sets, scored by success rate.*

An open-source simulated benchmark of 50 robotic manipulation tasks performed by one simulated Sawyer arm on a table-top, built so that a single policy can address every task: all tasks share a 39-dimensional observation space and a 4-dimensional action space (end-effector displacement and gripper). It was released with a CoRL 2019 paper and is now maintained by the Farama Foundation. The protocol is a set of task sets. MT1, MT10 and MT50 train one multi-task policy on 1, 10 or 50 tasks, with a one-hot task ID, and score it on the same tasks and goals. ML1 meta-trains on goal variations of one task and tests on held-out goals; ML10 and ML45 meta-train on 10 or 45 tasks and test few-shot adaptation on 5 held-out tasks. Each task has a success condition, typically the object within a distance threshold of its goal, and the reported number is the mean success rate over tasks and goal positions, an episode counting as a success if the condition held at any step. The environments changed without announced versions: the -v1 environments and rewards of 2019 gave way to -v2 environments with rewritten rewards, and Meta-World+ (release 3.0.0, 2025) moved to MuJoCo's own Python bindings and Gymnasium as -v3 environments, kept both reward functions selectable, and added MT25 and ML25. Its authors show that results under the two reward functions are not comparable. There is no leaderboard; results appear in papers, among them vision-language-action papers reporting on the MT50 tasks.

#### meta-world · Identity and id

- `self_description` · [S1][meta-world-s1]
  > Meta-World is an open source benchmark for developing and evaluating multi-task and meta reinforcement learning algorithms for continuous control robotic manipulation environments
- `released` = 2019-10-24 · [S2][meta-world-s2]
  > Submitted on 24 Oct 2019 (v1), last revised 14 Jun 2021 (this version, v2)
- `release_venue` = CoRL 2019 (3rd Conference on Robot Learning, Osaka); Meta-World+ at NeurIPS 2025 Datasets and Benchmarks · [S3][meta-world-s3]

#### meta-world · Domain and capabilities

- `domain` = primary robotics-embodiment/manipulation · [S4][meta-world-s4]
  - why: Every task is a simulated Sawyer arm changing the state of objects -- reaching, pushing, picking and placing, opening doors, drawers and windows -- and every episode is scored on whether the object reached its goal. The claim is about multi-task and meta-RL algorithms, which is the family's mujoco-gymnasium near miss; the entry keeps it here because the task distribution is defined by one robot body manipulating objects, the paper motivates it by robots acquiring skills, and the score is task success rather than a control objective (see review\_checks).
  > All of our tasks are performed by a simulated Sawyer robot.
- `capability` = sensorimotor-control · [S4][meta-world-s4]
  - why: A policy issues end-effector displacements and a gripper command to a simulated arm in closed loop, and the episode is scored on whether the resulting physical state meets the task's success condition.
  > The action space is a 2-tuple consisting of the change in 3D space of the end-effector followed by a normalized torque that the gripper
- `capability` = transfer-learning · [S4][meta-world-s4]
  - why: ML10 and ML45 meta-train on 10 or 45 tasks and score adaptation to 5 held-out tasks with new objects and interactions, the meta-test success reported apart from meta-training success -- the inclusion test's new tasks after earlier ones. It holds for those two task sets only (see subsets); ML1 varies only goal positions.
  > not just in terms of parametric variation in goals, but completely new objects and interaction scenarios
- `evaluation_method` = simulation-rollout · [S6][meta-world-s6]
  - why: Every reported number is the share of simulated episodes in which the task's success flag was set at any step, averaged over tasks and goal positions.
  > In Metaworld, agents are to be evaluated using their success rate on a set of tasks and goal positions, not the episodic reward achieved during training.
- `designed_for_subjects` = rl-policy · [S4][meta-world-s4]
  - why: The environments are built for policies trained by multi-task and meta-reinforcement learning; the paper's baselines (multi-task PPO, TRPO and SAC, task embeddings, RL2, MAML and PEARL) come from the authors' Garage library. Vision-language-action models now report on the MT50 tasks too (as\_used); rl-policy covers trained policies on a Benchmark either way.
  > We use the baselines in the Garage \[59\] reinforcement learning library, which we developed for benchmarking Meta-World.

Considered and rejected:

- `domain` not `general-intelligence/meta-learning` · [S5][meta-world-s5]
  - why: Its definition, how quickly a system improves across a distribution of related tasks, describes ML1, ML10 and ML45. But the general-intelligence exclusion sends a benchmark whose breadth lies inside one family to that family's subdomains, every task is manipulation by one arm, and the MT task sets score multi-task training, not adaptation.
  > Meta-World contains 50 different robotic manipulation tasks for a single Sawyer Robot Arm2 to solve.
- `domain` not `robotics-embodiment/continuous-control` · [S1][meta-world-s1]
  - why: The README calls the environments continuous control, but every task is scored on a semantic success condition, an object brought to its goal, not on a control objective, which the leaf's definition requires.
  > Meta-World is an open source benchmark for developing and evaluating multi-task and meta reinforcement learning algorithms for continuous control robotic manipulation environments
- `domain` not `robotics-embodiment/dexterous-manipulation` · [S4][meta-world-s4]
  - why: The gripper is commanded by one scalar beside the end-effector displacement; the difficulty is the breadth of tasks, not degrees of freedom, so the leaf's distinction keeps it under manipulation.
  > The action space is a 2-tuple consisting of the change in 3D space of the end-effector followed by a normalized torque that the gripper
- `domain` not `robotics-embodiment/embodied-instruction-following` · [S4][meta-world-s4]
  - why: A task is identified by a one-hot task ID in the multi-task sets and not at all in the meta-learning sets; there is no natural-language instruction.
  > In our experiments, the algorithm is typically provided with a one-hot vector indicating the current task.
- `capability` not `sample-efficiency` · [S6][meta-world-s6]
  - why: Few-shot adaptation is the meta-RL claim, and the evaluation pseudocode defaults to 10 adaptation episodes per test goal, but no budget of training samples or steps is fixed at which the score is taken, and the multi-task sets fix none at all.
  > adaptation\_steps = 1, adaptation\_episodes = 10, num\_evals = 40
- `capability` not `continual-learning` · [S7][meta-world-s7]
  - why: All training tasks are available at once in both the multi-task and the meta-training phase; nothing is presented in sequence and no retention is scored.
  > Unlike usual RL benchmarks, the training of the agent is strictly split into training and testing phases.
- `capability` not `compositional-generalization` · [S4][meta-world-s4]
  - why: Meta-World+ speaks of composing skills to adapt to unseen tasks, but the original paper says the held-out tasks bring completely new objects and interaction scenarios, which the term's exclusion (new primitives) leaves out.
  > not just in terms of parametric variation in goals, but completely new objects and interaction scenarios
- `capability` not `distribution-shift-generalization` · [S4][meta-world-s4]
  - why: ML1 tests on held-out goal and object positions within one task, which differ from training only by sampling, the term's exclusion; the held-out tasks of ML10 and ML45 change the task, which is transfer-learning.
  > meta-testing on 50 heldout positions
- `evaluation_method` not `episodic-return` · [S6][meta-world-s6]
  - why: Each task has a shaped dense reward (V1 or V2) for training, and the evaluation utilities also return mean returns, but the documentation rules out reward as the evaluation metric.
  > In Metaworld, agents are to be evaluated using their success rate on a set of tasks and goal positions, not the episodic reward achieved during training.

#### meta-world · Data and licence

- `as_used` = protocol Vision-language-action models report a success rate averaged over difficulty tiers of the MT50 tasks, not the designed protocol's mean over tasks and goal positions after multi-task RL training. · [S8][meta-world-s8]
  > achieving a tier-averaged success rate of 91.1% on Meta-World MT50
- `data.access` = fully-open · [S1][meta-world-s1]
  - why: The package, its environments and its evaluation utilities install from PyPI without an account.
  > To install Meta-World, use \`pip install metaworld\`
- `data.refresh` = versioned-releases · [S5][meta-world-s5]
  - why: The environments carry version suffixes (-v1, -v2, -v3) and the package has tagged releases (v2.0.0, 3.0.0, v3.1.1). The change from -v1 to -v2 was not announced as a release, which Meta-World+ was written to remedy.
  > This work highlights the need for explicit versioning of software benchmarks that researchers should report in their works.
- `data.data_provenance` = simulation-generated · [S4][meta-world-s4]
  > All of the tasks are implemented in the MuJoCo physics engine \[53\], which enables fast simulation of physical contact.
- `data.ceiling_anchor_type` = theoretical-maximum · [S4][meta-world-s4]
  - why: The headline is a success rate bounded at 1, every episode successful. The paper checked that each task can be solved by single-task RL, which shows the tasks are learnable one at a time, not that any task set's bound is reachable.
  > verify that each of the 50 presented tasks are indeed solveable by existing single-task reinforcement learning algorithms
- `data.size` = count 50; unit tasks · [S2][meta-world-s2]

  > The MT10 evaluation uses 10 environments: reach, push, pick and place, open door, open drawer, close drawer, press button top-down, insert peg side, open window, and open box.
- `data.size` = count 5; unit held-out test tasks, beside 10 or 45 meta-training tasks; subset ML10 and ML45 · [S1][meta-world-s1]
  > ML10 comprises 10 train tasks with 5 test tasks, while ML45 comprises of 45 training tasks with 5 test tasks.

**Open review checks** (9):

1. (field `domain`) Embodiment. Meta-World's claim is about multi-task and meta-RL algorithms, as mujoco-gymnasium's is about control algorithms, and the family's near miss excludes benchmarks whose embodiment is not the point. The entry keeps it in robotics-embodiment/manipulation because the tasks are object manipulation by one robot arm, scored on object state, and the paper motivates it by robots acquiring skills. general-intelligence/meta-learning as primary, or a machine-learning home the taxonomy lacks, is the alternative. · [S2][meta-world-s2]
   > Meta-reinforcement learning algorithms can enable robots to acquire new skills much more quickly
2. (field `lineage`) Farama maintenance is not a fork. The repository was transferred (created 2019-09-09, per the GitHub API), the README at v2.0.0 announces the Foundation as maintainer, and three original authors are on Meta-World+, so one Benchmark with a maintainer-changed event, not a lineage fork; confirm that the 04 S4 test (different maintainer) does not apply to a hand-over. · [S10][meta-world-s10]
   > Metaworld is now maintained by the Farama Foundation!
3. (field `versions`) version\_kind. v1 to v2 and v2 to 3.0.0 are revisions (the same 50 tasks and task sets, changed environments and rewards). 3.0.0 also renamed the environments, removed -v1 and added two task sets, so an edition reading is arguable. breaking is left false for 3.0.0 and 3.1.1 on the maintainers' reproducibility claim, which was not checked and which the move from mujoco-py to MuJoCo 3 makes uncertain. · [S5][meta-world-s5]
   > Through this process we release a new open-source version of Meta-World1 that has full reproducibility of past results
4. (field `versions`) The v2 version has no release date. Meta-World+ says the V1 rewards were overwritten at an unstated point; the first dated source read that reports the -v2 environments is the paper's 2021-06-14 revision, and the repository's history was not searched. · [S5][meta-world-s5]
   > However, at some point these V1 rewards were overwritten by a new set of dense rewards, which we will refer to as V2.
5. (field `versions`) 3.1.1 fixed the button-press dense rewards, so V2 training rewards for those tasks differ from 3.0.0; whether that makes 3.1.1 breaking for training-curve or success comparisons is not stated. · [S13][meta-world-s13]
   > dense rewards for button press fixed
6. (field `subsets`) Task-set counts disagree across sources. ML1's held-out goals are 50 in the paper and 10 in the documentation, and ML10 has 3 test tasks in the README at v2.0.0 but 5 in both papers and the current documentation. · [S10][meta-world-s10]
   > It comprises 10 meta-train tasks, and 3 test tasks.
7. (field `capability`) capability. transfer-learning rests on ML10 and ML45 alone, and the MT subsets override it away; multi-task learning, what MT10 and MT50 measure, has no term (taxonomy failure 2026-11-04-meta-world-001). sample-efficiency was rejected although few-shot adaptation is the meta-RL claim, because no training budget is fixed.
8. (field `comparability.material_extra`) comparability. The reward function version (V1 or V2) changes multi-task results and has no condition field; the entry records it inside harness. A reward\_function\_version field, or a reading of V1 and V2 under 3.x as subsets, is the alternative. · [S5][meta-world-s5]
   > These results are not comparable, as the two sets of reward functions have different design philosophies and per-task reward scales
9. (field `as_used`) as\_used. Vision-language-action papers report a tier-averaged MT50 success whose tiers no Meta-World source defines; how such policies are trained and which release they use was not read. · [S8][meta-world-s8]
   > achieving a tier-averaged success rate of 91.1% on Meta-World MT50

**Reviewer checklist** for `meta-world`:

- [ ] Identity and id: the name, aliases, id, paper and release date are right, and this is one benchmark, not a family or an edition of another
- [ ] Domain and capabilities: the primary and secondary subdomains, capabilities, evaluation methods and intended subjects fit, and no rejected term should have been kept
- [ ] Task and evaluation: the task, scoring, ground truth, entrants and harness read as the sources describe them
- [ ] Data and licence: access, refresh, provenance, sizes, subsets, contamination and licences match the sources
- [ ] Governance and independence: maintainer type, submission process, funding and independence flags are right
- [ ] Lifecycle and activity: lifecycle, activity, versions, editions and history are current
- [ ] Every open review check above is answered or resolved
- [ ] Nothing here would embarrass the catalogue in front of a specialist

**Evidence** (33 quoted fields), by checklist area:

#### bi-dexhands · Identity and id

- `self_description` · [S1][bi-dexhands-s1]
  > we propose the Bimanual Dexterous Hands Benchmark (Bi-DexHands), a simulator that involves two dexterous hands with tens of bimanual manipulation tasks and thousands of target objects
- `released` = 2022-06-17 · [S2][bi-dexhands-s2]
  > Submitted on 17 Jun 2022 (v1), last revised 11 Oct 2022 (this version, v2)
- `release_venue` = NeurIPS 2022 Track on Datasets and Benchmarks; a journal version in IEEE TPAMI 46(5), 2024 · [S1][bi-dexhands-s1]
  > 36th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2022) Track on Datasets and Benchmarks

#### bi-dexhands · Domain and capabilities

- `domain` = primary robotics-embodiment/dexterous-manipulation; secondary robotics-embodiment/bimanual-manipulation · [S1][bi-dexhands-s1]
  - why: Every task is manipulation by two simulated Shadow Hands, 24-DoF hands with 20 actuated tendon pairs each, and the paper places the difficulty in the high-dimensional actuation and the contact-rich model, which is the dexterous leaf's case. The benchmark's claim is also two-hand cooperation on tasks specified for the dual-hand embodiment (handing over, swapping two objects, holding a bottle in one hand and twisting its cap with the other), which the bimanual leaf records as secondary; it is not primary because its definition is two coordinated arms, and these hands sit on fixed or constrained floating bases with no arm (see review\_checks).
  > such dexterous manipulation remains a challenging problem because of the high dimensional actuation space and contact-rich model
- `capability` = sensorimotor-control · [S1][bi-dexhands-s1]
  - why: A policy issues joint-position targets to two simulated hands at 30 Hz in closed loop, the simulator responds, and the reward depends on where the object ends up relative to its goal.
  > For object-catching tasks, our reward is simply related to the difference between the pose of the object and the target.
- `capability` = transfer-learning · [S1][bi-dexhands-s1]
  - why: The meta-RL categories ML4 and ML20 train on 3 and 15 tasks and score adaptation to 1 and 5 held-out tasks, with train and test rewards reported separately; the test tasks are different tasks, not resampled goals, which is transfer-learning rather than distribution shift. ML1 and the multi-task categories vary only goals or train on all tasks, and do not carry the term.
  > ML4 and ML20 are categories for learning meta-policies in 3&15 tasks respectively and hoping to adapt to new 1&5 testing tasks.
- `evaluation_method` = episodic-return · [S1][bi-dexhands-s1]
  - why: The reported numbers are episode rewards -- learning curves for the 20 tasks, average reward for the multi-task and meta categories -- and offline scores normalised so that 100 is the expert policy's return, a reference that can be exceeded. The dense rewards have no stated maximum.
  > The average reward for each training is shown in Table 4.
- `designed_for_subjects` = rl-policy, multi-agent-system · [S1][bi-dexhands-s1]
  - why: The tasks are built for policies trained by reinforcement learning, with single-agent (PPO, TRPO, SAC), offline (BCQ, TD3+BC, IQL), multi-task and meta baselines. Multi-agent learners are a designed entrant of their own -- the README offers MARL algorithms (HAPPO, HATRPO, MAPPO, IPPO, MADDPG) and the paper runs each hand as an agent -- whose joint behaviour is what the shared reward scores.
  > Note that the experiments of MARL algorithms run based on two agents, which means each hand represents an agent.

Considered and rejected:

- `domain` not `robotics-embodiment/continuous-control` · [S1][bi-dexhands-s1]
  - why: Much of the benchmark's use is as a testbed for RL and MARL algorithms beside MAMuJoCo, the community the family's mujoco-gymnasium near miss describes. But each task is a semantic manipulation goal (open a door, lift a pot, stack blocks) on a named, human-like hand, and the paper's claim is human-level dexterity, so the embodiment is the point, which keeps the entry under manipulation rather than control in the abstract.
  > Our environments focus on the application of RL algorithms to dexterous hand control
- `domain` not `robotics-embodiment/sim2real-transfer` · [S1][bi-dexhands-s1]
  - why: Transfer to real hands is named as future work; nothing the benchmark scores runs on hardware.
  > We would like address the sim-to-real gap by transferring the simulation result on real dexterous hands.
- `capability` not `collaboration` · [S1][bi-dexhands-s1]
  - why: The multi-agent formulation splits the hands into agents, but it is a fully cooperative game with one shared reward that the paper says is completely inferable from the single-agent setting, and single-agent PPO controlling both hands is the strongest baseline. The coordination scored is one robot's two hands, recorded by the bimanual leaf, not agents working towards a shared outcome.
  > Therefore, the setting of multi-agent can be completely inferred from the setting of single-agent.
- `capability` not `sample-efficiency` · [S3][bi-dexhands-s3]
  - why: The baselines run 100M environment steps with 2,048 parallel environments, but that is the authors' training configuration; the benchmark fixes no budget at which entrants are scored.
  > All baselines are run under the parameters of \`2048 num\_env\` and \`100M total\_step\`.
- `capability` not `distribution-shift-generalization` · [S1][bi-dexhands-s1]
  - why: Every episode resets the object's start and goal poses at random, and objects can be swapped within a category; no score on deliberately shifted inputs is reported. ML1's held-out goals within one task are resampled goals, an ordinary split.
  > All environments are goal-based
- `evaluation_method` not `simulation-rollout` · [S3][bi-dexhands-s3]
  - why: The README's plan marks a success metric for all tasks as done, which would be a bounded outcome, but the paper reports rewards, and the README's own baseline figures are reward curves; which metric later users report was not surveyed (see review\_checks).
  > Success Metric for all tasks

### 2.3 RoboTwin (robotwin)

`data/benchmarks/robotics-embodiment/robotwin.yaml` · `verification_status: ai-drafted-unverified` · curator confidence medium · added 2026-10-14 · last verified 2026-10-14

*50 simulated dual-arm manipulation tasks, scored in clean and in domain-randomized scenes, with a standing leaderboard.*

A simulation benchmark and data generator for dual-arm (bimanual) manipulation. RoboTwin 2.0, the current version, has 50 dual-arm tasks built on an annotated library of 731 objects in 147 categories, expert demonstrations from task code that multimodal language models write and correct in simulation, five dual-arm embodiments, and domain randomization along five axes (clutter, lighting, background, tabletop height and instruction wording). The benchmark trains on 50 clean demonstrations per task on the Aloha-AgileX embodiment and scores success over 100 trials per task in clean scenes (Easy) and in domain-randomized ones (Hard). Its leaderboard, open since August 2025, ranks the paper's single-task baselines and policies co-trained on all 50 tasks by the mean of the two. RoboTwin 1.0 (2024-2025) had 15 tasks, with simulated and real-world data.

### 2.4 LocoMuJoCo (locomujoco)

`data/benchmarks/robotics-embodiment/locomujoco.yaml` · `verification_status: ai-drafted-unverified` · curator confidence medium · added 2026-11-04 · last verified 2026-11-04

*Imitation learning of locomotion from motion capture, on simulated humanoid, quadruped and human bodies in MuJoCo.*

A benchmark for imitation learning in locomotion, from TU Darmstadt's Intelligent Autonomous Systems Group and Locomotion Laboratory. Its first release (late 2023) had 12 environments built on MuJoCo -- the Talos, Atlas and Unitree H1 humanoids, the Unitree A1 quadruped, and a torque-actuated and a muscle-actuated human skeleton, each human model scalable to four ages -- and 27 tasks, each defined by a dataset of the behaviour to imitate: real, noisy motion capture retargeted to the robot (so the demonstrator's body differs from the agent's), ground-truth expert states and actions, and sub-optimal expert data. Each task has a handcrafted reward, such as matching a target forward velocity, used to evaluate rather than to train, and the experiment scripts report the mean undiscounted return over evaluation episodes; baselines are GAIL, VAIL, GAIfO, IQ-Learn, LS-IQ and SQIL. Version 1 (2025) is a rewrite on JAX with MuJoCo for single and MJX (since 1.1 also MuJoCo Warp) for parallel environments, 12 humanoid and 4 quadruped environments, over 22,000 motion capture datasets retargeted to each humanoid (its own, LAFAN1 and AMASS), JAX baselines (PPO, GAIL, AMP, DeepMimic) and trajectory metrics such as dynamic time warping. There is no leaderboard; results appear in users' papers.

- `self_description` · [S1][locomujoco-s1]
  > we present LocoMuJoCo, a Python-based benchmark tailored for locomotion within the context of imitation learning (IL)
- `released` = 2023-11-04 · [S2][locomujoco-s2]
  > Submitted on 4 Nov 2023 (v1), last revised 30 Nov 2023 (this version, v2)
- `release_venue` = NeurIPS 2023 Workshop on Robot Learning (Pretraining, Fine-Tuning, and Generalization with Large Scale Models) · [S1][locomujoco-s1]
  > NeurIPS 2023 Workshop on Robot Learning: Pretraining, Fine-Tuning, and Generalization with Large Scale Models

#### locomujoco · Domain and capabilities

- `domain` = primary robotics-embodiment/locomotion · [S1][locomujoco-s1]
  - why: Every task is a simulated legged body -- humanoid robots, a quadruped, human skeleton models -- moving across the ground without falling, and an episode ends when the body falls. The family's mujoco-gymnasium near miss does not fit. That benchmark's claim is control algorithms in the abstract; LocoMuJoCo is built against exactly that, faulting Gym-MuJoCo and the DeepMind Control Suite for toy tasks with dynamics tuned for RL, and it ships models of real robots (Talos, Atlas, Unitree H1, A1, and in 1.x G1, Go2, Spot, ANYmal C and others), motion capture retargeted to each body, and domain randomisation aimed at the sim-to-real gap. The embodiment is the point (see review\_checks).
  > Existing benchmarks for this setting either tackle toy tasks, are very far from realistic settings and real robotic platforms or are not designed for IL
- `capability` = sensorimotor-control · [S4][locomujoco-s4]
  - why: A policy issues actions to a simulated body in closed loop, the simulator responds, and the score is a reward computed on the resulting motion, such as how closely the centre of mass keeps the expert's velocity, accumulated until the episode ends or the body falls.
  > The default reward function is based on the distance between the current center of mass velocity and the desired velocity in the x-axis.
- `evaluation_method` = simulation-rollout · [S5][locomujoco-s5]
  - why: The reported number is the mean undiscounted return of the task's handcrafted reward over simulated evaluation episodes. The default reward, exp(-(v - v\_target)^2) on the forward velocity, is at most 1 per step, so an episode's return cannot exceed its length and the score is bounded; papers set the expert at 1000 (RILe).
  > which are the mean undiscounted return, mean discounted return, and the mean length of an episode the agent, respectively.
- `designed_for_subjects` = rl-policy · [S1][locomujoco-s1]
  - why: The entrants are imitation-learning algorithms, judged by the policies they train in the simulator -- adversarial imitation and inverse RL in the baselines, behaviour cloning at the simple end -- which rl-policy covers (LIBERO's entry tags behaviour-cloned policies the same way); a custom reward also makes it a pure RL benchmark.
  > we provide a set of baselines of classical IRL and adversarial IL approaches

Considered and rejected:

- `domain` not `robotics-embodiment/continuous-control` · [S1][locomujoco-s1]
  - why: The default score, matching a target centre-of-mass velocity, is a control objective, but the leaf holds continuous control in the abstract, which the family's near miss keeps apart; the paper sets itself against those benchmarks, and the tasks are gaits of specific bodies, which locomotion names.
  > Both of the benchmarks do not explicitly focus on the IL setting and only consider toy tasks with dynamics fine-tuned for RL.
- `domain` not `robotics-embodiment/whole-body-humanoid-control` · S3
  - why: The 1.x README calls the benchmark designed for whole-body control, and the humanoids imitate whole-body motions, but the leaf needs tasks where balance and manipulation cannot be solved separately. No task manipulates an object; the carry tasks hold a weight in front of the robot while it walks.
  > is an \*\*imitation learning benchmark\*\* specifically designed for \*\*whole-body control\*\*.
- `domain` not `robotics-embodiment/cross-embodiment-transfer` · [S1][locomujoco-s1]
  - why: The motion capture is of people and is retargeted to each robot, so demonstrator and agent differ in body, but that is a condition of learning; no policy trained on one body is scored on another.
  > Hence, we provide realistic motion capture datasets for all environments, which naturally come with embodiment mismatches
- `domain` not `robotics-embodiment/sim2real-transfer` · [S1][locomujoco-s1]
  - why: Domain randomisation is offered to reduce the sim-to-real gap, but nothing the benchmark scores runs on hardware.
  > LocoMuJoCo allows the users to easily include domain randomization, reducing the sim-to-real gap
- `capability` not `transfer-learning` · [S1][locomujoco-s1]
  - why: Learning from another body's demonstrations (human motion capture for a robot) is built in, but the task, objective and body are the same at training and scoring, and no transfer quantity is reported.
  > Hence, we provide realistic motion capture datasets for all environments, which naturally come with embodiment mismatches
- `capability` not `distribution-shift-generalization` · [S1][locomujoco-s1]
  - why: Dynamics randomisation and partially observable variants (a randomised carry weight hidden from the policy) are options a user switches on, not a held-out condition the benchmark scores. RILe's test setting with unseen initial positions is that paper's own protocol (see as\_used).
  > we construct Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (POMDP) environments by randomizing the carry weight
- `evaluation_method` not `episodic-return` · S6
  - why: The score is a return, but of a reward bounded at 1 per step; the term is for returns with no defined maximum.
  > return np.exp(- np.square(x\_vel - self.\_target\_vel))
- `evaluation_method` not `reference-metric` · S3
  - why: Version 1 adds trajectory comparison against the reference motion (Euclidean distance, dynamic time warping, discrete Frechet distance), but the term is for similarity to reference texts, and the release paper's metric is the task reward. No term covers a distance to a reference trajectory (taxonomy failure 2026-11-04-locomujoco-001).
  > Powerful \*\*trajectory comparison metrics\*\* including dynamic time warping and discrete Fréchet distance, all in JAX
- `designed_for_subjects` not `classical-algorithm` · [S1][locomujoco-s1]
  - why: The Unitree A1 datasets were generated with model predictive control, but MPC is the source of demonstrations, not an entrant.
  > we generated the datasets for the Unitree A1 using Model Predictive Control (MPC)

**Open review checks** (9):

1. (field `domain`) Scope. The family's mujoco-gymnasium near miss was weighed and judged not to fit -- the paper sets itself against Gym-MuJoCo and the DeepMind Control Suite for toy tasks and claims realistic robot platforms, motion capture and a sim-to-real aim. A reviewer may still read the benchmark's community as imitation-learning algorithm research in the abstract, which would make it the near miss. · [S1][locomujoco-s1]
   > Both of the benchmarks do not explicitly focus on the IL setting and only consider toy tasks with dynamics fine-tuned for RL.
2. (field `domain.secondary`) whole-body-humanoid-control was rejected as a secondary because no task manipulates objects, although the 1.x README says the benchmark is designed for whole-body control and the carry tasks load the arms. · S3
   > is an \*\*imitation learning benchmark\*\* specifically designed for \*\*whole-body control\*\*.
3. (field `versions`) Versions. 1.x is modelled as an edition of the same benchmark (same maintainer and repository, same task of imitating recorded locomotion, new environments, datasets, algorithms and metrics). The 04 S4 call is not clear-cut -- the rewrite keeps few of 0.x's 27 task definitions as such, and a revision or a new entry are the alternatives. · S9
   > Explore a new collection of 12 humanoid and 4 quadruped environments.
4. (field `evaluation_method`) simulation-rollout rests on the default reward exp(-(v - v\_target)^2) being at most 1 per step, read in the v0.1.0 code; other tasks' rewards and the 1.x reward classes were not read, and if any is unbounded the method is episodic-return. 1.x also adds trajectory distances, which may be what newer papers report. · S6
   > return np.exp(- np.square(x\_vel - self.\_target\_vel))
5. (field `lifecycle`) Evidence of current use is thin. RILe's results are in a 2025 revision of a 2024 paper; TRIRL (2026) uses LocoMuJoCo's motion capture for its G1 environments, but the sources do not show whether its environments are LocoMuJoCo's, and one of its authors is a LocoMuJoCo author. No 2025-2026 paper was found reporting on the 1.x environments or metrics. · [S13][locomujoco-s13]
   > motion capture dataset and train using a state-based discriminator
6. (field `governance.maintainer_type`) maintainer\_type individual follows the vocabulary's personal-account rule (repository, datasets and documentation under the first author's accounts); academic-lab (TU Darmstadt IAS) is the alternative if the lab is taken to hold it.
7. (field `data.dataset_licence`) dataset\_licence CC-BY-NC-ND-4.0 is the Hugging Face card's tag for the 1.x repository. The LAFAN1 folder says its licence differs from Unitree's original, whose file was not read; AMASS and SMPL-H come under their own non-commercial terms, which were not read or accepted; the 0.x datasets' licence was not found. · S14
   > This dataset is distributed under a different license than the original Unitree dataset.
8. (field `task`) The current (1.x) documentation could not be read because /en/latest/ is disallowed by robots.txt; task, reward and evaluation facts come from the paper and the 0.x documentation, and 1.x facts from the repository only. · [S4][locomujoco-s4]
   > Walking: The robot has to walk forward with a fixed speed of 1.25 m/s.
9. (field `data.size`) The 1.x size of over 22,000 datasets counts AMASS motions retargeted per humanoid, which users must obtain under AMASS's terms; the Hugging Face repository itself holds 19 default and 40 LAFAN1 datasets per humanoid. Which count is the headline for 1.x is a judgement. · S3
   > \*\*Over 22,000 motion capture datasets\*\* (AMASS, LAFAN1, native LocoMuJoCo) retargeted for each humanoid

### 2.5 HumanoidBench (humanoidbench)

`data/benchmarks/robotics-embodiment/humanoidbench.yaml` · `verification_status: ai-drafted-unverified` · curator confidence medium · added 2026-11-04 · last verified 2026-11-04

*27 whole-body locomotion and manipulation tasks for a simulated Unitree H1 humanoid with dexterous hands, in MuJoCo.*

A simulated benchmark for learning whole-body humanoid control, from the Robot Learning Lab (RLL) at UC Berkeley, with Yonsei University, published at RSS 2024. The robot is a Unitree H1 humanoid with two Shadow Hands, simulated in MuJoCo, with 61 position-controlled actuators driven at 50 Hz; models of the Unitree G1, Agility Digit, a Robotiq gripper and Unitree hands are also provided. There are 12 locomotion tasks (walk, run, hurdle, stairs, a maze, balancing on an unstable board and others) and 15 whole-body manipulation tasks (pushing a box, opening cabinets, unloading a truck, catching and throwing a basketball, in-hand cube reorientation, peg insertion and others), 31 environments counting the simple and hard variants. Each task has a dense, hand-designed reward and an episode limit of 500 or 1,000 steps, and the paper reports episode return per task beside a per-task target that marks success qualitatively. The default observation is the privileged robot and object state; egocentric cameras and whole-body tactile sensing are available but were not benchmarked. The paper's baselines (DreamerV3, TD-MPC2, SAC, PPO and a hierarchical policy) stay below the target on most tasks. There is no leaderboard; results appear in users' papers.

#### humanoidbench · Identity and id

- `self_description` · [S1][humanoidbench-s1]
  > we present a high-dimensional, simulated robot learning benchmark, HumanoidBench, featuring a humanoid robot equipped with dexterous hands
- `released` = 2024-03-15 · [S2][humanoidbench-s2]
  > Submitted on 15 Mar 2024 (v1), last revised 18 Jun 2024 (this version, v2)

#### humanoidbench · Domain and capabilities

- `domain` = primary robotics-embodiment/whole-body-humanoid-control; secondary robotics-embodiment/locomotion, robotics-embodiment/dexterous-manipulation · [S1][humanoidbench-s1]
  - why: Every task is scored on a full humanoid whose legs, arms and hands are controlled together, and the manipulation tasks are built so that balance and manipulation cannot be separated -- the paper's door failure is the robot pulling with its arm without moving its body back. taxonomy/domains.yaml gives this benchmark as the family's qualifying example. Locomotion is secondary for the 12 locomotion tasks (hurdle, stairs, slides, a pole forest, a tunnel), which the paper offers as easier tasks and primitive skills. Dexterous manipulation is secondary for the tasks whose difficulty is the hands' degrees of freedom -- in-hand reorientation of two cubes, and inserting a peg into two tight blocks.
  > Before learning any manipulation skills, an agent must learn locomotion skills to balance and move towards an object or the world to interact.
- `capability` = sensorimotor-control · [S1][humanoidbench-s1]
  - why: A controller issues joint-position targets for 61 actuators at 50 Hz, the simulator responds, and the score is the reward the resulting physical behaviour earns. taxonomy/capabilities.yaml gives this benchmark as the term's qualifying example.
  > For both position and torque control, the action space is 61-dimensional including the two hands, and controlled at 50 Hz.
- `evaluation_method` = episodic-return · [S1][humanoidbench-s1]
  - why: Every reported number is a return, the sum of a task's hand-designed rewards over an episode (average and maximum returns over three seeds in the appendix tables). No source read states a maximum, and the per-task targets mark success qualitatively rather than bounding the scale; on stand the best runs (about 930) exceed the target of 800.
  > Returns are computed by summing the rewards at all timesteps of an episode.
- `designed_for_subjects` = rl-policy, classical-algorithm · [S1][humanoidbench-s1]
  - why: The environments are built for trained policies -- the paper's baselines are model-based and model-free reinforcement learning and a hierarchical policy over pretrained reaching skills -- and the paper says they support any controller, model-based control among them, without benchmarking one. A non-learned entrant has since been evaluated, model-predictive control with MuJoCo MPC (src-arxiv-2408-00342), which classical-algorithm covers.
  > While we do not benchmark classical model-based control approaches \[14, 26\] in this work, our environments support actions obtained by using any type of controllers.

Considered and rejected:

- `domain` not `robotics-embodiment/bimanual-manipulation` · [S1][humanoidbench-s1]
  - why: Several tasks use both hands (package, insert, cube), but the claim is whole-body control of a humanoid, and the paper sets its benchmark apart from bimanual ones; the leaf's exclusion covers two arms incidental to another setting.
  > While bimanual manipulation is one of the key objectives of humanoid robots, most benchmarks in humanoid research have so far focused on the locomotion challenges
- `domain` not `robotics-embodiment/continuous-control` · [S1][humanoidbench-s1]
  - why: The tasks are scored on hand-designed dense rewards, which is near the leaf's definition, but the embodiment is the point -- a model of real hardware with real hands -- which is what separates this benchmark from the family's mujoco-gymnasium near miss.
  > This motivates us to implement a comprehensive simulated humanoid benchmark based on real-world hardware
- `domain` not `robotics-embodiment/mobile-manipulation` · [S1][humanoidbench-s1]
  - why: Some tasks need the robot to move and manipulate (truck, room, door), but on legs and with balance as the difficulty, which whole-body-humanoid-control names more narrowly.
  > truck: Unload packages from a truck by moving them onto a platform.
- `domain` not `robotics-embodiment/navigation` · [S1][humanoidbench-s1]
  - why: One task (maze) asks the robot to reach a goal through turns, but from privileged state, with nothing to perceive or map.
  > maze: Reach the goal position in a maze by taking multiple turns at the intersections.
- `domain` not `robotics-embodiment/tactile-sensing` · [S1][humanoidbench-s1]
  - why: Whole-body tactile sensing (448 taxels) is implemented, but the benchmark's results use state observations only, and touch is not the primary input of any scored task.
  > we first focus on the state-based environment setup, where proprioceptive robot states and object states are used as the
- `domain` not `robotics-embodiment/sim2real-transfer` · [S1][humanoidbench-s1]
  - why: The paper names sim-to-real transfer as future work; nothing is run on hardware.
  > show promise to study sim-toreal transfer in more depth
- `capability` not `long-horizon-execution` · [S1][humanoidbench-s1]
  - why: The paper stresses long-horizon tasks, and a fall ends the episode, but the score is a return that accumulates over the episode, most tasks are tracking or posture objectives rather than sequences of dependent steps, and nothing has to be remembered from earlier in the episode under the state-based setup.
  > All the baseline algorithms perform below the success threshold on most tasks, particularly struggling on tasks that require long-horizon planning
- `capability` not `sample-efficiency` · [S1][humanoidbench-s1]
  - why: The paper reports returns at 10M (DreamerV3, SAC) and 2M (TD-MPC2) environment steps, but those budgets came from giving each method about 48 hours of compute; the benchmark fixes no step budget at which performance is scored.

**Open review checks** (9):

1. (field `evaluation_method`) evaluation\_method is episodic-return because the paper reports returns with no stated maximum. Many tasks' per-step rewards lie in \[0, 1\] over a fixed 1,000-step limit, which would bound them, and later papers may report success against the targets instead; simulation-rollout is the alternative, and it changes no comparability profile. · [S1][humanoidbench-s1]
   > Returns are computed by summing the rewards at all timesteps of an episode.
2. (field `domain`) dexterous-manipulation is secondary on three of 31 environments (cube, insert\_small, insert\_normal) and on the hands being part of every task; dropping it, leaving locomotion as the only secondary, is the alternative. · [S1][humanoidbench-s1]
   > cube: Manipulate two cubes in-hand until they both reach a randomly initialized target orientation.
3. (field `versions`) The 0.1 and 0.2 package versions are modelled as revisions with the same 31 items; the tags and their dates come from the GitHub API, not a quoted Source, and the 0.1 entry's released date is the repository's first commit. Whether a balance-reward change under unchanged ids merits versions at all, or only an erratum, is a modelling call. · S9
   > bounds=(\_STAND\_HEIGHT + 0.35, float("inf")),
4. (field `execution.compute_tier_note`) Which MuJoCo version produced the paper's results is not stated; the first commit (2024-03-18) left mujoco unpinned, and the 3.1.6 pin appears by the v0.1.0 tag (2024-06-29). · S7
   > "mujoco==3.1.6",
5. (field `execution.reproducibility_blockers`) Later papers often run HumanoidBench through GPU-parallel reimplementations rather than this package; whether those are the same benchmark (and should be lineage forks) was not checked.
6. (field `data.contamination_risk_note`) The MuJoCo MPC paper finds the sparse rewards produce unrealistic behaviour when optimised and adds regularisation terms, so a return can rise without the intended behaviour; a construct-validity note for a reviewer, not a field. · [S10][humanoidbench-s10]
   > We find that sparse reward functions of HumanoidBench yield undesirable and unrealistic behaviors when optimized
7. (field `designed_for_subjects`) classical-algorithm rests on the paper's statement that any controller is supported and on one non-learned entrant (MuJoCo MPC, 2024), which evaluated a subset of tasks with its own regularised reward. · [S10][humanoidbench-s10]
   > Current evaluations on a subset of tasks
8. (field `governance.maintainer_type`) maintainer\_type academic-lab rests on setup.py and the LICENSE naming RLL at UC Berkeley; the code sits in the first author's personal account, so individual is the alternative if the lab does not maintain it. The 2025 BAIR Commons line in the LICENSE was not followed up. · S8
   > This software is part of the BAIR Commons HIC Repository as of calendar year 2025.
9. (field `homepage`) The site says 27 tasks and is the homepage here; the README links a copy on the first author's personal domain, which was not read. · [S11][humanoidbench-s11]
   > HumanoidBench is the first-of-its-kind simulated humanoid robot benchmark, including 27 distinct whole-body control tasks

### 2.6 Room-to-Room (R2R) (r2r)

`data/benchmarks/robotics-embodiment/r2r.yaml` · `verification_status: ai-drafted-unverified` · curator confidence medium · added 2026-11-05 · last verified 2026-11-05

*Crowd-written route instructions followed in unseen Matterport3D buildings, scored by success rate and SPL.*

The first benchmark for vision-and-language navigation in real buildings (CVPR 2018). An agent is placed in a building it has not seen, in the Matterport3D Simulator, and must follow a crowd-written route instruction (on average 29 words) to the goal and stop there. The simulator is built from the Matterport3D scans, 10,800 panoramic RGB-D views of 90 buildings, and the agent moves between panoramic viewpoints along a navigation graph, adjusting its camera heading and elevation; actions are deterministic. The 7,189 paths are shortest paths of 4 to 6 edges sampled on that graph, each with three Amazon Mechanical Turk instructions (21,567 in all). An episode succeeds if the agent stops within 3 m of the goal, measured along the graph, and the path taken is not scored. Success rate and SPL are the primary metrics, beside navigation error, trajectory length and oracle success. The splits are train (61 buildings), val-seen (the same buildings), val-unseen (11 buildings) and test (18 buildings); test goals are withheld, and participants run their agent locally and submit trajectories to a server on EvalAI that has been open since 2018. Crowd workers reached 86.4% success on the test set and the first seq2seq baseline 20.4%. R4R, RxR and VLN-CE, all by other maintainers, grew out of it and are separate benchmarks.

#### r2r · Domain and capabilities

- `domain` = primary robotics-embodiment/navigation; secondary robotics-embodiment/embodied-instruction-following · [S3][r2r-s3]
  - why: The scored outcome is whether the agent, moving through a building it must perceive as it goes, stops within 3 m of a goal location, which is the navigation leaf's definition. The goal is given only through a natural-language route instruction, so embodied-instruction-following is secondary. That leaf was weighed as primary (calvin takes it so) and lost, because the score is where the agent stops, not whether the instructed route was carried out, and R4R was built by other authors to score that fidelity (lineage). The same call as aerialvln in this round.
  > We consider an episode to be a success if the navigation error is less than 3m.
- `capability` = grounding · [S3][r2r-s3]
  - why: The instruction is a referring description of a route and goal in a presented world, and success is whether the agent reached the location it describes. The benchmark's own claim is the interpretation of visually grounded instructions in previously unseen real imagery, which distinguishes it from the libero near miss, whose sources never claim grounding. See review\_checks (aerialvln rejected the term).
  > What distinguishes the VLN challenge is that the agent is required to interpret a previously unseen natural-language navigation command in light of images generated by a previously unseen real environment.
- `capability` = distribution-shift-generalization · [S3][r2r-s3]
  - why: Val-unseen (11 buildings) and test (18 buildings) are buildings held out from the 61 training buildings, and results are reported for val-seen and val-unseen side by side; the paper reports the seen-unseen gap as its most surprising result.
  > (38.6% vs. 21.8% success for studentforcing)
- `evaluation_method` = simulation-rollout · [S6][r2r-s6]
  - why: Episodes are run in the Matterport3D Simulator (by the participant, for the test split), and each is a success or a failure, with SPL bounded by 1; navigation error and trajectory length are distances reported beside them. The EvalAI server scores the submitted trajectories against the withheld goals and does not run a simulator itself.
  > The primary evaluation metrics of interest are Success Rate (success), and Success rate weighted by normalized inverse Path Length (SPL).
- `designed_for_subjects` = rl-policy · [S3][r2r-s3]
  - why: The simulator is presented as a reinforcement-learning environment, and the release's entrants are navigation policies trained on the training split (the seq2seq baseline by teacher- and student-forcing; DUET and NavGPT-2 backbones in the 2026 paper read), which rl-policy's test covers as learned controllers acting in the environment.
  > The simulator is a large-scale interactive reinforcement learning (RL) environment constructed from the Matterport3D dataset

Considered and rejected:

- `capability` not `sensorimotor-control` · [S4][r2r-s4]
  - why: The agent teleports between panoramic viewpoints on a precomputed navigation graph with deterministic actions; there is no dynamics, collision or localisation error in the loop. VLN-CE was built to drop exactly these assumptions.
  > Specifically, our setting drops the presumptions of known environment topologies, short-range oracle navigation, and perfect agent localization.
- `capability` not `instruction-following` · [S5][r2r-s5]
  - why: The paper claims instruction following as the task, but the score is the stop location; compliance with the described route is not checked (the term's exclusion for answer-only scoring), which is the shortcoming R4R's authors raise.
  > We also show that the existing paths in the dataset are not ideal for evaluating instruction following because they are direct-to-goal shortest paths.

**Open review checks** (10):

1. (field `domain`) Primary navigation, secondary embodied-instruction-following. R2R is the founding vision-and-language navigation benchmark and the task statement fits both leaves; navigation leads because only the stop location is scored. calvin, the instruction-following leaf's entry, scores whole chains of instructions; aerialvln in this round made the same call as here. · [S3][r2r-s3]
   > as many instructions do not specify the path that should be taken
2. (field `domain.primary`) Whether robotics-embodiment holds at all. The agent teleports between panoramas on a navigation graph with deterministic actions and no dynamics, which is why sensorimotor-control was rejected; the family's exclusion ("symbolic with no body") was judged not to apply because the agent has a pose and camera in real imagery. A reviewer may prefer a note that VLN-CE is the embodied form. · [S4][r2r-s4]
   > this setting lifts a number of assumptions implicit in prior work that represents environments as a sparse graph of panoramas with edges corresponding to navigability
3. (field `capability`) grounding is tagged on the paper's own claim (visually grounded instructions), although the score is the stop location; aerialvln rejected grounding on the libero near miss for the same kind of score. The two entries should agree.
4. (field `lineage.forks`) Lineage. R4R and VLN-CE reuse R2R's items under other maintainers, so they are forks under 04 S4. RxR shares no items, only the simulator, buildings and task, and R2R's first author is among its authors; it could instead be unrelated in lineage, or noted only as a successor dataset. Ids r4r, rxr and vln-ce are proposed here, and none has an entry. · [S13][r2r-s13]
   > We introduce Room-Across-Room (RxR), a new Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN) dataset.
5. (field `governance.maintainer_type`) maintainer\_type individual rests on the repository and Dropbox links sitting in one person's accounts; the site's copyright line names the Australian Centre for Robotic Vision, which would make it academic-lab if that centre is taken as the holder. · [S1][r2r-s1]
   > © 2018 Australian Centre for Robotic Vision.
6. (field `data.ceiling_anchor_type`) The best system row (84.6% success, 0.801 SPL, June 2026) has reached the crowd workers' 86.4% success and passed their SPL. saturated is derived and needs claims; the headroom left is small. · [S8][r2r-s8]
   > "result":\[10.703935932157377,1.74210147454204,0.8727534148094895,0.8461538461538461,0.8011862326141211\]
7. (field `data.submission_limit`) The submission limit is stated per user (5 in all, one a day), while EvalAI enforces limits per participant team; the guidelines forbid extra accounts. Leaderboard rows are not verified by the host (no row is marked verified), and the beam-search rows from before the rule are still listed. · [S6][r2r-s6]
   > the number of submissions per user is limited to 1 upload per day and a maximum of 5 submissions per user
8. (field `designed_for_subjects`) designed\_for\_subjects is rl-policy only. Zero-shot agents on prompted language models are widely reported on R2R validation subsets, but no source read here shows one; observed\_subjects could add agent-scaffold once one is read.
9. (field `data.dataset_licence`) dataset\_licence follows the README (Matterport3D terms cover data derived from the scans). The terms were not opened, so whether the R2R instruction files themselves are under them is the README's statement only.
10. (field `versions`) No versions are recorded. The simulator's v0.1 tag (2018) and its February 2019 release differ in API, not in R2R's items; whether results depend on the simulator release is not stated, so it is carried in comparability rather than as a version. · S9
   > to mark the first release we have tagged it as \[v0.1\]

#### behavior-1k · Domain and capabilities

- `domain` = primary robotics-embodiment/mobile-manipulation · [S4][behavior-1k-s4]
  - why: A robot must move through house-scale scenes, across rooms, and manipulate many objects in them within one task; the paper's own keyword is mobile manipulation.
  > BEHAVIOR tests whether embodied agents can combine high-level reasoning, long-horizon navigation, and dexterous bimanual manipulation in house-scale scenes
- `capability` = sensorimotor-control · [S5][behavior-1k-s5]
  - why: A policy server receives the robot's observations and returns an action at every step, the simulator responds, and the score is the physical state the episode ends in.
  > the policy server is responsible for receiving observations and returning robot actions
- `capability` = long-horizon-execution · [S4][behavior-1k-s4]
  - why: One episode is a whole activity -- search across rooms, many objects, state changes -- over minutes of closed-loop control, and the simplest activities in the paper already need 6 to 16 primitive steps. Some state changes cannot be undone (the paper marks slicing irreversible), so a wrong action can make full success unattainable; partial credit for satisfied predicates does not disqualify the term (ADR-0020). The paper also finds memory of the agent's own earlier progress decisive ("it needs additional information to know what location has been cleaned already").
  > satisfy symbolic BDDL goal conditions after several minutes of autonomous execution
- `evaluation_method` = simulation-rollout · [S5][behavior-1k-s5]
  - why: Each rollout runs in OmniGibson and is scored on a bounded scale, the fraction of the task's goal predicates satisfied at episode end, averaged over tasks.
  > Partial successes = (Number of goal BDDL predicates satisfied at episode end) / (Total number of goal predicates)
- `designed_for_subjects` = rl-policy, classical-algorithm · [S4][behavior-1k-s4]
  - why: The challenge is built for closed-loop controllers of any method. Learned policies -- imitation, reinforcement learning, robot foundation models such as the pi0.5 and GR00T N1.7 baselines -- are rl-policy; task and motion planning, named beside them and allowed by the rules, can enter with no learned component, which classical-algorithm covers (ADR-0020 settled this benchmark's subjects as both).
  > The 2026 challenge is intended as a shared benchmark for testing robot foundation models, imitation learning, reinforcement learning, task and motion planning, memory systems, SLAM, and LLM-assisted policies

- `domain` not `robotics-embodiment/bimanual-manipulation` · [S5][behavior-1k-s5]

### 2.8 nuPlan (nuplan)

`data/benchmarks/robotics-embodiment/nuplan.yaml` · `verification_status: ai-drafted-unverified` · curator confidence medium · added 2026-11-05 · last verified 2026-11-05

*Planners driven through about 1,300 hours of real logs, scored open-loop and in non-reactive and reactive closed loop.*

Motional's benchmark and dataset for autonomous-vehicle motion planning. The dataset is about 1,300 hours of manually driven logs from Las Vegas, Boston, Pittsburgh and Singapore, auto-labelled offline with object tracks, traffic-light states inferred from other vehicles' motion and 73 mined scenario types, on human-annotated HD maps; 128 hours carry raw lidar and camera data. A planner receives the ego state, the route, tracked agents and map information (current and 2 s past), and returns a trajectory of at least 8 s every 0.1 s within a 1 s budget, over scenarios of up to 15 s. The devkit scores it in three modes. Open-loop compares the planned trajectory with the human driver's. Closed-loop non-reactive tracks it with an LQR controller and a kinematic bicycle model while the other agents replay their logs. Closed-loop reactive does the same with vehicles driven by the Intelligent Driver Model. Each scenario's closed-loop score multiplies penalties (at-fault collisions, drivable area, driving direction, making progress) by a weighted average of time to collision, progress along the expert's route, speed-limit compliance and comfort, in \[0, 1\]. The 2023 nuPlan Planning Challenge (CVPR 2023) took Docker images on EvalAI, ran them on a hidden test set over 14 scenario types and ranked by the mean of the three modes. The leaderboard closed after the challenge; since then results are computed locally with the devkit on the public splits, most often other groups' Val14 and Test14 selections in the two closed-loop modes.

| Classification | |

- `lineage.forks` = id navsim; maintainer Autonomous Vision Group, University of Tübingen, with co-authors (see navsim.yaml) · [S13][nuplan-s13]

- `lineage.forks` = id interplan; maintainer The interPlan authors (arXiv 2404.07569) · [S14][nuplan-s14]

#### nuplan · Domain and capabilities

- `domain` = primary robotics-embodiment/autonomous-driving-planning · [S3][nuplan-s3]
  - why: The entrant is a driving planner and the score is the driving outcome of its trajectories -- at-fault collisions, drivable-area and driving-direction compliance, progress, speed limits, comfort -- not perception accuracy, which is the leaf's definition. The family's inclusion test asks for an outcome produced by embodied action, here driving a simulated vehicle in closed loop through real logged scenes.
  > we propose the world's first closed-loop ML-based planning benchmark for autonomous driving.
- `capability` = planning · [S1][nuplan-s1]
  - why: The entrant outputs a planned trajectory, which the open-loop mode scores directly against the human driver's and the closed-loop modes hand to the benchmark's own controller; the benchmark's claim is planning.
  > To assert kinematic feasibility and prevent users from cheating, we require the use of a controller.
- `capability` = sensorimotor-control · [S4][nuplan-s4]
  - why: In the two closed-loop modes, which carry the community's results, the planner is queried again every 0.1 s on the state its earlier trajectories produced, and in the reactive mode the other vehicles respond to the ego. The score is that driven behaviour, so the loop is closed through the entrant, unlike NAVSIM's single query (see review\_checks).
  > The simulation horizon will be up to 15s for each scenario and the simulation frequency will be 10Hz.
- `evaluation_method` = simulation-rollout, domain-metric, composite · [S4][nuplan-s4]
  - why: Each closed-loop scenario is a simulated episode scored on a bounded scale, with penalties that can zero it times a weighted average of graded sub-scores, as CARLA's driving score is (simulation-rollout). The open-loop mode scores displacement and heading errors and the miss rate against the logged expert trajectory within bounds, motion-planning measures (domain-metric). The challenge ranked the mean of the three modes' scores (composite).
  > The submissions are ranked based on the mean overall score across all three challenges.
- `designed_for_subjects` = rl-policy, classical-algorithm · [S1][nuplan-s1]
  - why: The benchmark targets ML-based planners, mostly trained by imitation on nuPlan's logs (the Urban Driver baseline; the diffusion and transformer planners of 2026), scored by acting in closed loop, which subjects.yaml calls rl-policy (as for CARLA). Rule-based planners are entered beside them -- the IDM baseline, PDM-Closed in the 2026 tables -- and the 2023 challenge's best closed-loop planner was mostly rule-based, which is classical-algorithm.
  > It is evident that sufficiently sophisticated rule-based planners still outperform purely learned planners in closed-loop settings.

Considered and rejected:

- `domain` not `vision/driving-perception-3d` · [S4][nuplan-s4]
  - why: The dataset carries lidar and camera data and auto-labelled 3D tracks, but planners receive tracked objects and nothing perceptual is scored.
  > that includes ego pose, ego route, agents, and static/dynamic map information.
- `capability` not `distribution-shift-generalization` · [S1][nuplan-s1]
  - why: The paper studies covariate shift in closed loop and city transfer (training on Las Vegas, testing elsewhere), but these are experiments, not scored conditions; the benchmark's splits are stratified across days, cities and scenarios.
  > to minimize temporal data leakage, data from the same day and city is not shared across splits.
- `evaluation_method` not `constraint-check` · [S5][nuplan-s5]
  - why: The multiplier metrics (at-fault collision, drivable area, driving direction, making progress) invalidate a scenario, but they are judged on the simulated execution, which the term excludes; simulation-rollout carries them.
  > there is an at\_fault collision with a vehicle or a VRU (pedestrian or bicyclist), or
- `designed_for_subjects` not `task-specific-supervised-model` · [S1][nuplan-s1]
  - why: The open-loop mode scores learned planners on logged data without acting, which is this term, but the closed-loop modes, which carry the headline use, have them act in simulation.
  > We train the model using imitation learning to match expert trajectories available in the nuPlan dataset.

#### nuplan · Task and evaluation

- `learned_entrant_evidence` = system ExecDiffuser (diffusion planner) · [S8][nuplan-s8]
  > ExecDiffuser achieves the best overall performance across the six nuPlan settings, with an average score of 85.62
- `learned_entrant_evidence` = system DriveMLP (imitation-learned planner) · [S10][nuplan-s10]
  > It achieves a score of 86.51 on the nuPlan Val14 Reactive benchmark
- `reproducible_by_third_party` = true · [S7][nuplan-s7]
  - why: The dataset, including the test split's logs and labels, and the devkit are public (after registration), and since the leaderboard closed the field's results are computed that way. The 2023 challenge's scores on the hidden test set cannot be reproduced.
  > As the online leaderboard submission is closed, all evaluations are conducted on the nuPlan public test set.
- `task` = exists true; input the ego pose and its 2 s history, the route to the mission goal, the tracked agents and objects (vehicles, pedestrians, cyclists, cones, barriers, signs, generic objects), and the static and dynamic map, including traffic-light states, at each 0.1 s iteration, optionally lidar and camera data, released for 128 hours of the logs; output A trajectory of at least 8 s of rear-axle poses (x, y, heading, time) in the global frame, every iteration within a 1 s budget. In the closed-loop modes an LQR tracker and a kinematic bicycle model propagate the ego along it for the next step.; scoring Per scenario, closed-loop (CLS-NR, CLS-R) = the product of no at-fault collisions (0, 0.5, 1), drivable-area compliance, driving-direction compliance (0, 0.5, 1) and making progress, times the weighted average of time to collision (5), progress along the expert's route (5), speed-limit compliance (4) and comfort (2). Open-loop (OLS) = miss rate within bound times the weighted average of ADE, FDE, AHE and FHE within bound, over 3, 5 and 8 s horizons. Each mode's score is the mean over scenarios; the challenge ranked the mean of the three.; metric_range 0, 1 · [S5][nuplan-s5]
  > A planner is assigned a score between 0 and 1 based on its performance in multiple scenarios.

  > We implement a Linear Quadratic Regulator (LQR) \[72\], \[73\] as the tracker.

  > The Planning Challenge will be using devkit version 1.2 from now on.
- `execution.harness` = motional/nuplan-devkit (nuplan.planning simulation, metrics and nuBoard; the submission engine in nuplan/submission for the challenge) · [S5][nuplan-s5]

**Open review checks** (11):

1. (field `capability`) Capability. planning and sensorimotor-control are both tagged. sensorimotor-control's tie-break sends a trajectory tracked by the benchmark's own controller in a non-reactive simulation to planning, which describes the CLS-NR mode literally; but nuPlan re-queries the planner every 0.1 s on the state it produced, and the reactive mode closes the loop through other vehicles too. A reviewer may keep planning only. · [S4][nuplan-s4]
   > Each planner will have a fixed time budget of 1s for each simulation iteration, after which the simulation will time out.
2. (field `evaluation_method`) evaluation\_method adds domain-metric and composite for the open-loop mode and the challenge's mean of the three modes, beside simulation-rollout; current papers report the closed-loop modes only, so simulation-rollout alone may be the better reading.
3. (field `lineage`) Val14 and Test14 are recorded as as\_used protocols, not forks, because they are scenario lists over nuPlan's own splits scored unchanged; 04 S4's "independently versioned and cited" could make them separate benchmarks, especially Test14-hard, whose selection depends on a planner (PDM-Closed). interPlan is a fork on its abstract alone. · [S16][nuplan-s16]
   > across the Val14, Test14-hard, and Test14-random community splits in both non-reactive and reactive modes
4. (field `versions`) Versions. The dataset releases are modelled (v0.1 and v1.0 editions, v1.1 a revision of the same logs) and the devkit versions are a condition (simulator\_version). v1.1 is unfrozen because the sensor data was to be released gradually; whether it completed was not checked. The devkit version used by 2026 papers is not stated in any source read. · [S2][nuplan-s2]
   > Submissions generated from version v1.1 should remain compatible.
5. (field `activity`) activity is closed. EvalAI's record ends on 2025-11-15 (inactive, frozen), but the PDM and PlanTF papers describe the leaderboard as closed in 2023. When submissions actually stopped, between 2023-05-26 and 2025-11-15, is unclear; the history's closing date follows the competition page. · [S6][nuplan-s6]
   > Unfortunately, due to the closure of the leaderboard
6. (field `data.access`) data.access is gated-registration for the released splits behind current results; the challenge's hidden test set made that round private-test-server. Whether the hidden set is the same as the released test split was not established.
7. (field `governance.independence_flags`) prize-sponsored-by-industry rests on the competition page's prizes and the terms' statement that Motional AD Inc. conducted the competition; no sentence says who paid. The maintainer type rests on the same legal-form wording. · [S9][nuplan-s9]
   > which is conducted by Motional AD Inc. and its affiliates
8. (field `task`) The scoring document lists driving\_direction\_compliance with a weight of 5 in its table while its text and the 2024 paper (Tables II and XIV) treat it as a multiplier; task.scoring follows the paper. · [S5][nuplan-s5]
   > \|driving\_direction\_compliance \|Score is 1 if during the previous \`time\_horizon\`
9. (field `known_limitation`) The 2024 paper notes that reactive agents use an IDM similar to the IDM baseline planner, which may favour it in closed loop; no source measures the bias. · [S1][nuplan-s1]
   > It should be noted though that the reactive agents are also modelled with a similar IDM.
10. (field `governance.participation`) The challenge's ranking table in the 2024 paper names team "CS Tu" first (0.895), while the PDM paper says PDM-Hybrid ranked first of 25 teams; that these are the same entry is likely but not stated. The EvalAI leaderboard itself was not read (it lists entrants by team names, some personal). · [S1][nuplan-s1]
   > Overall Score 0.895 0.875 0.848 0.829
11. (field `lineage`) The NAVSIM fork row cites navsim's Source src-github-navsim-splits, which needs nuplan in its cited\_by. navsim.yaml has no lineage block; it may want a fork role pointing here.

**Reviewer checklist** for `nuplan`:

- [ ] Identity and id: the name, aliases, id, paper and release date are right, and this is one benchmark, not a family or an edition of another

### 2.9 safe-control-gym (safe-control-gym)

`data/benchmarks/robotics-embodiment/safe-control-gym.yaml` · `verification_status: ai-drafted-unverified` · curator confidence medium · added 2026-11-05 · last verified 2026-11-05

*PyBullet cart-pole and quadrotor control tasks with constraints and disturbances, comparing control and RL on safety.*

An open-source benchmark suite from the University of Toronto's Dynamic Systems Lab (now the Learning Systems and Robotics Lab of TU Munich and the University of Toronto), built to compare learning-based control and reinforcement learning on the same footing. It extends the Gym API with symbolic a priori dynamics, cost and constraints (CasADi), and with configurable disturbances on control inputs, state measurements, inertial parameters and external forces such as wind, all simulated in PyBullet. The paper (IEEE RA-L 2022) has three unstable systems -- the cart-pole, and a 1D and a 2D quadrotor -- and two tasks, stabilisation and trajectory tracking (circle, sinusoid, lemniscate or square references); the current code adds a 3D quadrotor, and the quadrotor model is the Bitcraze Crazyflie 2.0. Results are read on control performance (RMSE to the reference, a quadratic cost or return), data efficiency, constraint violations and robustness to disturbances and parameter mismatch, with baselines from classical control (PID, LQR, iLQR, linear and nonlinear MPC), learning-based control (GP-MPC), RL (PPO, SAC, DDPG), safe and robust RL (safety layer, RARL, RAP) and safety filters (MPSC, CBF). There is no leaderboard. In 2022 the lab ran the IROS Safe Robot Learning Competition on a branch of the repository: a Crazyflie 2.x flies through gates to a goal under randomised dynamics and gate positions, scored in four simulated levels and a sim2real level on real Crazyflies.

#### safe-control-gym · Domain and capabilities

- `domain` = primary robotics-embodiment/drone-uav; secondary robotics-embodiment/continuous-control · [S1][safe-control-gym-s1]
  - why: Three of the four systems are quadrotors (1D, 2D and, in the current code, 3D) modelled on the Crazyflie 2.0, whose tasks are defined by flight dynamics (thrust, mass, inertia, wind) and by state and input constraints on the vehicle; the competition the suite hosted flies Crazyflies through gates in simulation and on hardware. The family's mujoco-gymnasium near miss was weighed. Its claim is control algorithms in the abstract; safe-control-gym's is safe control for deployment on real robots, with real robots' models, disturbances that mimic their non-idealities, and a sim2real competition, so the embodiment is the point. Continuous control is the secondary because the score is a control objective (tracking error, cost, constraint violations), and the cart-pole is not aerial (its subset overrides the primary). See review\_checks.
  > These correspond to the cases in which the movement of a quadrotor is constrained to the 1D motion in the vertical z-direction and the 2D motion in the xz-plane, respectively
- `capability` = sensorimotor-control · [S1][safe-control-gym-s1]
  - why: A controller or policy issues thrusts or forces to a simulated body in closed loop, the PyBullet simulation responds, and the score is the resulting motion against the reference.
  > it is important to clarify that we focus on safe, low-level control rather than vision-based applications
- `capability` = constraint-satisfaction · [S4][safe-control-gym-s4]
  - why: The benchmark's own claim includes satisfying constraints, every step's info reports constraint evaluations, and the experiment class scores the failure rate -- the share of episodes with any violation -- beside the number of violating steps; in the competition only runs with no collision or violation complete the task.
  > Occurence of any violation in episodes.
- `capability` = distribution-shift-generalization · [S1][safe-control-gym-s1]
  - why: The paper reports robustness as a condition of its own -- controllers evaluated against pole lengths and input noise away from those they were designed or trained for -- and the disturbance and randomisation API exists to build such conditions; Fuz-RL evaluates under the suite's perturbations at test time.
  > capability to satisfy constraints (Figure 7), as well as robustness against disturbances and parametric uncertainty (Figure 8)
- `evaluation_method` = simulation-rollout, physical-trial · [S5][safe-control-gym-s5]
  - why: The suite's results come from episodes in PyBullet, scored per episode on RMSE to the reference, constraint-violation counts and a failure rate (bounded in \[0,1\]), and a return whose default quadrotor reward is bounded in \[0,1\] per step. The competition's fifth level flew each entrant's controller on real Crazyflies in a motion-capture arena, and that level is scored like the simulated ones, which makes it a scored physical track, not a one-off validation.
  > \| sim2real \| \*\*Yes\*\* \| Real-life hardware \| \*\*Yes\*\*, injected \| \*No\* \| Sim2real transfer \|
- `designed_for_subjects` = rl-policy, classical-algorithm, physical-robot-system · [S1][safe-control-gym-s1]
  - why: The suite is built so that RL agents and non-learned controllers are scored on the same axes -- PPO, SAC and safe RL beside PID, LQR, iLQR and MPC -- with learning-based control (GP-MPC) and safety filters in between. The competition's sim2real level runs each entrant's controller on the organisers' Crazyflies, which physical-robot-system covers when every entrant gets the same body.
  > Our benchmark suite includes, as baselines, standard statefeedback controllers such as the linear quadratic regulator (LQR) and iterative LQR (iLQR)

Considered and rejected:

- `domain` not `robotics-embodiment/sim2real-transfer` · [S1][safe-control-gym-s1]
  - why: The suite itself is simulation only, by design; sim2real is scored only in the 2022 competition, whose subset carries it as a secondary.
  > While we acknowledge the importance of eventual real-robot experiments, here, we focus on simulation as a way to lower the barrier of entry and appeal to a larger fraction of the control and RL communities.
- `capability` not `adversarial-robustness` · [S1][safe-control-gym-s1]
  - why: RARL and RAP train against an adversary, but the evaluation's perturbations (parameter mismatch, white noise) are not selected to defeat the controller under test.
  > RAP is trained against adversarial input disturbances
- `evaluation_method` not `episodic-return` · [S6][safe-control-gym-s6]
  - why: The experiment class reports an average return, but the quadrotor's default reward is the exponentiated negative quadratic cost, bounded per step, and the paper's headline numbers are RMSE and constraint violations.
  > If to exponentiate negative quadratic cost to positive, bounded \[0,1\] reward.
- `evaluation_method` not `statistical-fit` · [S1][safe-control-gym-s1]
  - why: RMSE is a general statistic, but here it measures a closed-loop trajectory produced in the simulator, which simulation-rollout covers; nothing is predicted against observations.
  > Evaluation cost is the RMSE with respect to the target state(s).
- `evaluation_method` not `entrant-relative-ranking` · [S7][safe-control-gym-s7]
  - why: The 2022 competition gave 20, 10 and 5 points to the top three per level, so its final classification depends on the field; the quantities ranked (task time, violations, learning time) are absolute, and the suite has no ranking. See review\_checks.
  > the top 3 solutions ranked by safety and performance and the top 3 solutions ranked by data & compute efficiency were given 20, 10, and 5 points respectively
